title: Karna's abandonment
hook: a girl in a king's house is given a mantra by a sage, and tries it on the sun
carry: I only wanted to see if it worked

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the birth of the cousins: rough play, a poisoned meal, and a grudge that started young.

Two days ago, Kunti told Pandu about a sage's mantra, and held one piece back. Today the poem steps back in time to tell it. Before Kunti was a queen, she was a girl called Pritha, raised in the house of a king named Kuntibhoja. When the sage Durvasa came as a guest, the hard work of looking after him fell to her, and she did it well. His gift was the mantra. Now she is young, unmarried, alone with words that can summon a god.
screen: `PRITHA, IN KUNTIBHOJA'S HOUSE.` → `DURVASA'S GIFT.` → `DO THE WORDS WORK?`

segments.voice: With the mantra, Durvasa told her, she could call any god she liked, and that god would come and give her a son. Then he left. And the text says that, out of curiosity, she tries it. She looks up at the rising sun and speaks the mantra. And Surya, the sun god, comes. Here the story slows down, because Pritha is frightened. She tells him she only wanted to see if the gift worked. She's a girl in her father's house; she asks him to go. Surya answers that a god called by this mantra can't return for nothing. A son will be born. But he promises her something too: she'll remain a maiden afterward, her honor kept. So, at the week's end, the story hands us a beginning older than all the others. Before the five brothers, before the cousins, Kunti had a son. Nobody in the palace knows it. Notice how human the scene is. There's no villain in it: a sage's gift, a girl's curiosity, a god who keeps the rules of the mantra, and fear. Out of that fear, over the next few days, will come a choice that echoes through the whole poem.
screen: `A SAGE'S GIFT: A MANTRA.` · `SHE TRIES IT ON THE SUN.` · `SURYA COMES, AND SHE IS AFRAID.` · `A SON BEFORE ALL THE OTHERS.` · then, large: `NOBODY IN THE PALACE KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you started lately, maybe a little out of curiosity, the way Pritha tried those words. Don't decide yet whether it was wise; just look at it, and see where it might lead. If you like, rest your attention on the morning light, wherever it fell for you today.
Karna's abandonment. It begins here: a mantra from Durvasa, a girl's curiosity, and the sun answering her call.
Your line: I only wanted to see if it worked. A week of births ends with the oldest secret. That's day seven hundred twenty-eight.
